title: Grant Deed vs. Quitclaim Deed in California: What's the Difference?
content_html:
Why the Type of Deed Matters

A deed is the written document used to transfer ownership of real property from one person or entity to another. In California, the two deed types you'll encounter most often are the grant deed and the quitclaim deed. Both can convey an interest in real property, and deeds used in real estate transfers are commonly recorded with the county — but the two forms carry very different legal assurances about what the person signing actually owns. Understanding that difference matters whether you're buying a home, changing how title is held after a divorce, or adding a family member to title.

What a Grant Deed Is

A grant deed is the standard deed used in most California home sales. When a conveyance uses the word "grant," California law implies two covenants from the seller (the grantor), unless the deed's own express terms limit them.[1] First, that before signing, the grantor has not already conveyed the same estate — or any right, title, or interest in it — to anyone other than the buyer (the grantee). Second, that at the time of signing, the property is free from encumbrances done, made, or suffered by the grantor or anyone claiming under the grantor. These implied covenants can be enforced as if they had been written into the deed.[1]

In practical terms, a grant deed tells the buyer: "I haven't already transferred this property to someone else, and I haven't burdened it with liens or other encumbrances beyond what this deed itself excepts." Those covenants are limited to the grantor's own conduct and people claiming under the grantor — they are not a promise that no one else in the property's history ever created a problem.

Because of these built-in assurances, grant deeds are the norm in arm's-length purchase transactions — the kind most buyers and sellers go through when a home changes hands on the open market.

What a Quitclaim Deed Is

A quitclaim deed works differently. The California Supreme Court has described the basic idea of a quitclaim deed as transferring "whatever present right or interest the grantor has in the property."[2] The grant deed covenants described above are implied from the use of the word "grant,"[1] and a quitclaim deed does not carry comparable implied title covenants: it does not warrant that the grantor owns the property, or that title is free of liens or other defects. If the person signing holds no interest, there is no interest for the quitclaim deed to pass.

That makes a quitclaim deed an unusual choice for an arm's-length sale, where a buyer paying market value typically wants deed-based assurances about what they're getting. Quitclaim deeds are more often encountered where the parties already know the property's history and need to document a change in how title is held — for example:

  • Releasing a spouse's or ex-spouse's interest as part of a divorce or property settlement
  • Adding or removing a family member on title
  • Some transfers into or out of a living trust
  • Clearing up a "cloud" on title, such as an old interest someone may still claim
  • Gifts of property between family members

These are situations where a quitclaim deed may be used — not situations where it is automatically the right instrument. Depending on the transaction, a grant deed or another instrument may be used instead, and the choice can have title and lending consequences worth discussing with the escrow officer, the title company, or a real estate attorney before anything is signed.

Side-by-Side: The Core Difference

The clearest way to think about the distinction: a grant deed carries statutory implied covenants about the grantor's own prior conveyances and encumbrances,[1] while a quitclaim deed passes whatever present interest the grantor has, without comparable covenants.[2] Neither deed form guarantees that the property is free of every lien, unpaid tax, or title defect created by anyone at any time. A title search and title insurance are separate from the deed itself.

A few mechanics apply to both. Under California law, a grant takes effect upon delivery by the grantor.[3] Before a deed can be recorded, its execution must be acknowledged — the notarized acknowledgment you see on recorded deeds.[4] And recording matters because an unrecorded conveyance is generally void against a later good-faith purchaser or lender for value whose own conveyance is recorded first.[5] The recording step itself is covered in our article on what documents get recorded at closing in Riverside County.

A Common Misconception: Quitclaim Deeds and Mortgages

Transferring an ownership interest by quitclaim deed does not by itself change who owes a mortgage or other loan secured by the property. Under California law, the burden of an obligation can generally be transferred only with the consent of the party entitled to its benefit — here, the lender.[6] So a spouse or co-owner who quitclaims their interest may remain liable on the loan unless the lender agrees otherwise, such as through a refinance or a lender-approved assumption.

Why a Buyer Should Care Which Deed They're Getting

If you're purchasing a home through a standard sale, you should expect to receive a grant deed. A quitclaim deed showing up in a purchase transaction — especially one where you're paying full market value — is a signal to slow down and ask why. It could reflect a title question the seller is uncertain about, or simply the wrong form being used. Either way, it's worth raising with your agent, escrow officer, or a real estate attorney before moving forward.

Deed covenants are only one layer of protection. The title company's search of the public record and the title insurance policy issued at closing are separate protections, and what a policy covers depends on its terms and listed exceptions — our article on what title insurance is and what California homebuyers should know explains how that works. If you're in the middle of a purchase, our guide to what to expect during escrow walks through where the deed fits in the closing timeline.

Why a Seller Should Care Too

If you sign a grant deed, the covenants implied from the word "grant" can be enforced against you as if they had been written into the deed.[1] If it later turned out that you had already conveyed an interest to someone else, or had encumbered the property yourself without that encumbrance being excepted in the deed, those covenants could expose you to a claim. A quitclaim deed, which passes only whatever present interest the grantor has,[2] does not carry comparable implied covenants — one reason it is often considered for transfers between family members or in a divorce settlement, where the parties are not making an arm's-length sale. Whether it is the right instrument still depends on the transaction.

Other Deed Types You Might Encounter

Grant deeds and quitclaim deeds are the two you'll see most often, but they are not the only instruments. Other instruments may be used for transfers involving spouses or trusts, depending on the transaction. If you're unsure which applies to your situation, it's worth a conversation with a real estate attorney or, for sale transactions, your real estate agent or escrow officer, before signing anything.

Bottom Line

A grant deed and a quitclaim deed can both convey an interest in real property, but they are not interchangeable. A grant deed carries statutory implied covenants about the grantor's own prior conveyances and encumbrances, which is why it is the standard choice for arm's-length home sales. A quitclaim deed passes whatever present interest the grantor has without those covenants, and is more commonly seen in transfers between parties who already know the property's history. Neither deed replaces a title search and title insurance, and neither one, by itself, changes who owes the mortgage.

mainEntity.name: Is a quitclaim deed less secure than a grant deed?

acceptedAnswer.text: A quitclaim deed provides fewer deed-based assurances. A grant deed carries implied covenants under California Civil Code section 1113 that the grantor has not already conveyed the property to someone else and has not encumbered it, unless the deed's express terms limit those covenants. A quitclaim deed transfers whatever present interest the grantor has, without comparable covenants. Neither deed replaces a title search or title insurance.

mainEntity.name: Can a quitclaim deed be used to buy a home in California?

acceptedAnswer.text: A quitclaim deed can transfer whatever interest the grantor has, including in a sale. In practice, grant deeds are the standard in arm's-length home purchases because a quitclaim deed does not carry the implied covenants that come with a grant deed. A buyer offered a quitclaim deed in a purchase should ask why and raise it with their escrow officer, title company, or a real estate attorney.

mainEntity.name: Does either deed guarantee the property is free of liens?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A grant deed's implied covenants cover only encumbrances done, made, or suffered by the grantor or anyone claiming under the grantor, and a quitclaim deed carries no comparable covenants. Protection against other liens and title defects depends on the title search and the title insurance policy, including its exceptions.

mainEntity.name: Does signing a quitclaim deed remove someone from the mortgage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not by itself. A quitclaim deed can transfer whatever ownership interest the grantor has, but it does not by itself change who owes the loan. Under California law, the burden of an obligation can generally be transferred only with the consent of the party entitled to its benefit, so a borrower typically remains liable unless the lender agrees otherwise.
